outcomes: The same migration set produces the same schema in the same order on a laptop, in CI, and in production
A migration either applied or did not: there is no state where the DDL committed and the record did not
Editing a migration that already ran is caught at the next run instead of drifting silently
Two instances starting at once do not both migrate, whichever language they are written in
A long DDL or backfill is not killed by the timeout that protects request-serving queries
nonGoals: Choosing an authoring format: this runner consumes what the SQL source contributes
Rolling forward past a failed migration, or repairing a schema the runner did not create
Cross-datasource atomicity: each datasource migrates under its own lock and transaction
Promising that a pre-1.0 minor release keeps the previous migration contract

requirements.text: Migrations apply in plain code-unit order of their name — byte-identical to the Go runner and the bundle protocol — never in locale-dependent collation order, because both runners share one state store.
Rollback, rollback-to, and reset reverse that same name order rather than ordering by execution timestamp, which is unstable for a batch applied inside one millisecond or under clock skew.
A migration's body and its success row commit in one transaction, so a failure between the two cannot leave a schema change that the next run would apply again.

A failed migration rolls its body back, records the failure outside the rolled-back transaction as a best effort, logs one terminal record, and aborts the run with a typed `MigrationError` naming the migration.
An already-applied migration whose committed SQL no longer hashes to the stored hash fails the run with both hashes, instead of being skipped by name as a plain forward apply would.
Stored rollback SQL is verified against its stored hash before it runs, and the state row is claimed before the down body executes so a concurrent runner cannot roll the same migration back twice.
Every migration operation holds a PostgreSQL advisory lock keyed on the datasource, hashed server-side from the same literal the Go runner uses, so concurrent starts serialize across languages.

`statement_timeout` is disabled transaction-locally for a migration body and for a rollback body, so a long DDL is not aborted by the pool's request-serving timeout, and the setting reverts at COMMIT or ROLLBACK rather than leaking onto the pooled connection.

A datasource that declares a schema applies it as a transaction-local `search_path` around each body, so one migration set can target several schemas with unqualified DDL, while the state store stays fully qualified.
A migration named by bare basename resolves only when it is unique; an ambiguous basename fails with the candidate list rather than picking one.
